nodes.principle: Enforce stringent server-side authorization checks, centralized access control logic, secure failure modes, role-based access policies, and regular re-validation of user privileges to prevent unauthorized access and privilege escalation.

Implement secure, centralized authentication mechanisms that enforce strong password management, ensure credentials are hashed and stored securely, safeguard against credential-related vulnerabilities, and utilize multi-factor authentication for high-value transactions.

Implement robust TLS for all sensitive data transmission, enforce certificate validity and integrity, prevent downgrade to insecure channels, and define character encodings while managing URL parameters to eliminate exposure of sensitive information.

Ensure cryptographic operations run on trusted server environments; master secrets are securely managed and accessed; error handling in cryptographic modules is secure; approved random generators are used; compliance with FIPS 140-2 is maintained; and key management policies follow formal lifecycle processes.
Implement strict access controls, secure data transmission, encryption at rest, and proper data deletion procedures to protect sensitive data from unauthorized access and exposure.
Employ strong typing and parameterized queries, validate and encode inputs, enforce least privilege through controlled access, and minimize attack surfaces across database interactions.

Implement robust error handling and logging practices that prevent sensitive data exposure, ensure user-friendly feedback, enforce strict access controls on logs, and maintain detailed records for security monitoring.

Implement rigorous validation, sanitization, and access controls for file uploads and inclusions, restrict execution capabilities, and ensure uploaded files are scanned for malware to mitigate attacks such as Local File Inclusion, Remote File Inclusion, and unauthorized file access.
Employ well-tested libraries and APIs, verify code integrity, minimize privilege duration, use proper synchronization, avoid direct user data execution, and rigorously assess third-party components.

Thoroughly validate all inputs for type, length, format, range, and whitelisting; enforce server-side checks, canonicalization, and strict character set usage to prevent injection attacks and data tampering.

Implement secure input validation, buffer size checks, proper resource management, safe string operations, and explicit memory deallocation to prevent buffer overflows, memory leaks, and code injection vulnerabilities.
Ensure safe output encoding for untrusted data across contexts like HTML, JavaScript, SQL, XML, and operating system commands to prevent injection attacks.

Implement robust session management through server-side controls, cryptographically secure identifiers, strict cookie attributes, and session invalidation to prevent fixation, hijacking, and CSRF attacks.
Maintain updated systems and configurations, enforce least privilege, secure exception handling, minimize attack surfaces, and audit security settings for robust operational integrity.
Always validate all inputs on a trusted server rather than relying on client-side validation.
Rigorously identify and classify all data sources as trusted or untrusted, then strictly validate all data originating from untrusted sources before processing.
All input must be validated through a centralized routine to ensure consistent enforcement of type, length, format, and whitelisted values before use.
Always specify appropriate character sets for input to ensure data integrity and prevent security vulnerabilities.
Always canonicalize input data to a consistent, common character set before performing any validation or security checks.
Any input that fails validation checks must be unconditionally rejected and not processed further.
Always perform input validation after fully decoding UTF-8 encoded data to prevent bypass attacks that exploit encoding ambiguity.
All client-supplied data—including query parameters, request bodies, URLs, HTTP headers, and cookie values—must be validated before being processed by the application.
Ensure all HTTP header values in requests and responses consist solely of ASCII characters.
Always validate all input data received via redirects to prevent malicious content submission and potential bypass of application logic.
Ensure that inputs match the expected data types to prevent vulnerabilities.
All input data must be validated to ensure it falls within an expected and acceptable range of values before being processed.
Always validate the length of input data to prevent buffer overflows, truncation, and resource exhaustion.
Always validate all input against a strict whitelist of allowed characters and patterns to prevent injection and other input-based attacks.
Implement additional controls when allowing potentially hazardous characters as input to prevent security vulnerabilities.
All user inputs must be validated and canonicalized to block null bytes, newline characters, and path traversal attempts, including both direct and obfuscated representations.
All output encoding must be performed on a trusted, server-side system to prevent injection vulnerabilities.
Always use well-tested, context-aware output encoding routines to prevent injection attacks.
Always apply context-appropriate output encoding to any untrusted data before returning it to the client to prevent injection attacks.
All output data must be encoded for the target interpreter context, allowing only explicitly whitelisted safe characters to pass through unencoded.
Always encode untrusted output to prevent injection attacks in SQL, XML, or LDAP queries.
Always sanitize or avoid passing untrusted data to operating system commands to prevent command injection attacks.
Implement authentication for all resources unless explicitly designated as public.
Authentication mechanisms should always be enforced on a secure server environment.
Always use well-established, thoroughly tested authentication libraries and services rather than implementing custom authentication mechanisms from scratch.
Centralize authentication into a single, reusable module to ensure consistent and secure management.
Authenticate users through a centralized mechanism rather than embedding authentication logic within individual resources.
Authentication controls must be designed to fail securely, denying access by default rather than granting it.
Administrative functions should match or exceed the security of user authentication mechanisms.
Store passwords exclusively as cryptographically strong, uniquely salted one-way hashes using modern algorithms, and restrict write access to the credential store to the application process only.
Hash passwords exclusively on a secure, trusted server environment using a modern, adaptive algorithm.
Authentication credentials must be validated only after all required input has been fully collected, preventing partial-input oracle attacks in sequential authentication flows.
Avoid disclosing specific details in authentication failure responses.
All connections to external systems handling sensitive information or critical functions must be properly authenticated.
Authentication credentials must be securely encrypted and stored in a trusted server-side location, not hardcoded in source code.
Authentication credentials must always be transmitted exclusively via HTTP POST requests, never via GET requests or other methods that expose credentials in URLs.
Only transmit non-temporary passwords over encrypted connections or as encrypted data, allowing for exceptions for temporary passwords used in secure reset processes.
Enforce robust password complexity requirements, aligned with established security policies and regulatory standards, to effectively resist common credential-based attacks.
Enforce minimum password length requirements (at least 8 characters, ideally 16 or more, or equivalent passphrase strength) as mandated by policy or regulation.
Password input fields must always obscure entered characters on screen to prevent shoulder-surfing and visual exposure of credentials.
Implement account lockout that disables user accounts after a defined number of failed login attempts to balance brute-force protection with denial-of-service prevention.
Password reset and change workflows must enforce the same stringent authentication, authorization, and protective controls as account creation and login.
Use password reset questions that require high-entropy answers and avoid easily guessable questions.
Send password reset instructions exclusively to a verified pre-registered email address using a secure, time-limited token.
Temporary passwords and links must expire quickly to enhance security.
Users must change their temporary passwords immediately upon first successful login.
Notify users whenever a password reset occurs to confirm the activity and help detect unauthorized resets.
Enforce a password history policy that prevents users from reusing recently used passwords during credential updates.
Enforce a minimum age requirement of at least one day for password changes to prevent immediate reuse attacks.
Enforce mandatory password expiration and rotation intervals according to organizational policy, with stricter schedules for critical systems.
Always disable "remember me" functionality for password fields to enhance security and prevent credential leakage.
Notify users about their account's last activity upon successful login.
Implement monitoring to detect and block credential stuffing and password-spraying attacks where a single password is used across multiple user accounts.
Always change or disable vendor-supplied default credentials before deploying any system or application to prevent unauthorized access.
Always require user re-authentication for critical actions to enhance security.
Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for highly sensitive or high-value transactional accounts to enhance security.
Thoroughly vet, audit, and continuously monitor all third-party authentication components for vulnerabilities and malicious code.
Always utilize robust, built-in session management controls to validate system-generated session identifiers.
Session identifiers must be generated and managed exclusively by trusted server-side systems to prevent forgery and unauthorized access.
Use cryptographically secure, well-vetted algorithms to generate unpredictable session identifiers.
Restrict cookie scope by setting the domain and path for session cookies to the site's exact host and minimal path, and enforce Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes.
Logout functionality must completely invalidate and destroy the server-side session and all associated tokens to prevent unauthorized reuse.
Logout functionality must be accessible from every page that requires authorization and must terminate the user's session to revoke access.
Enforce a short, risk-based session inactivity timeout to mitigate unauthorized access.
Terminate active sessions periodically and disallow persistent logins to reduce the risk of unauthorized access.
Always terminate pre-login sessions and generate a new session ID after successful user authentication to protect against session fixation attacks.
Always create a new session identifier during re-authentication to prevent session fixation and hijacking.
Enforce a single active session per user by invalidating any existing session upon a new login with the same user ID.
Session identifiers must never be exposed in URLs, error messages, or logs, and should only be transmitted via secure HTTP cookie headers.
Implement strict access controls to ensure server-side session data is only accessible by authorized users.
Regularly regenerate session identifiers and invalidate old ones to mitigate the risk of session hijacking.
Always generate a new session identifier when a connection transitions from HTTP to HTTPS to prevent session fixation.
Implement strong session management using unique random tokens for sensitive operations to prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks.
Utilize strong random tokens for each sensitive operation request to enhance security beyond session-level authentication.
Always set the 'Secure' attribute on session cookies to ensure they are only transmitted over encrypted TLS connections.
Always use the HttpOnly attribute on cookies to prevent access via client-side scripts unless script access is explicitly required.
Access authorization decisions must rely exclusively on trusted server-side objects, never on client-supplied data.
Implement a single, centralized component for all access authorization checks across the application.
Access controls must fail securely by denying access when checks fail without revealing sensitive details or compromising security state.
Always deny access when security configuration cannot be verified.
Authorization checks must be enforced server-side on every incoming request regardless of its origin, including AJAX calls, server-side includes, and script-generated requests.
Privileged logic must be distinctly separated from non-privileged application code to mitigate privilege escalation risks.
Access to files and resources, including those outside the application's direct control, must be restricted to authorized users only.
Access to protected URLs must be restricted to authorized users through stringent server-side checks.
Ensure that only authorized users can access protected functions and resources.
Ensure that direct object references are only accessible to authorized users.
Access to services must be limited to authenticated and authorized users only.
Access to application data should be limited to authenticated and authorized users only.
Limit visibility and access to sensitive user attributes, data attributes, and policy information critical for access control decisions.
Access to security-sensitive configuration information must be restricted to properly authorized users only.
Ensure consistency between server-side access control rules and their presentation layer representations.
Secure client-stored state data with encryption and server-side integrity checks to prevent tampering.
Application logic must enforce defined business rules and authorization checks to ensure secure access control.
Enforce per-user or per-device transaction rate limits to mitigate automated abuse while ensuring legitimate usage.
Do not rely on the Referer header as the sole authorization mechanism; it can be spoofed and should only serve as a supplemental check.
Periodically re-validate user authorization during long sessions.
Regularly audit accounts and automatically disable unused or expired accounts within a defined maximum period (e.g., 30 days after password expiration).
Applications must immediately disable accounts and invalidate all active sessions whenever a user's authorization status changes, such as role reassignment, termination, or business process changes.
Service accounts and accounts used for external system connections must operate with the least privilege necessary to perform their tasks.
Establish and maintain a formal Access Control Policy that defines business rules, data types, and authorization criteria to properly provision and enforce access to system resources.
Cryptographic operations protecting user secrets must always be performed on a trusted server-side system.
Master secrets must be securely stored and accessed only by authorized entities to prevent unauthorized disclosure or tampering.
Cryptographic modules must fail securely to prevent the exposure of sensitive information or compromise of operations upon error.
Use approved cryptographic random generators for any un-guessable random values.
All cryptographic modules must comply with FIPS 140-2 or an equivalent validated standard to ensure security and correctness.
Establish and enforce a formal policy and lifecycle process for cryptographic key management.
Avoid disclosing sensitive information in error messages.
Ensure error handlers do not expose sensitive debugging information.
Use generic error messages to avoid exposing sensitive information while providing a consistent user experience.
Applications must implement their own robust error handling mechanisms instead of relying on server defaults.
Always free allocated memory on all code paths, including error paths, to prevent memory leaks.
Error handling in security controls must always default to denying access or operations.
Ensure all logging operations are performed on a secure, trusted system to protect integrity and confidentiality.
Ensure comprehensive logging of all security-relevant events, including both successful operations and failures.
Logs must capture comprehensive contextual data to enable effective security monitoring, incident response, and debugging.
Sanitize all untrusted data before writing it to logs to prevent it from executing as code in log-viewing interfaces.
Ensure that log files are accessible only to authorized users and protected against unauthorized access.
Centralize all application logging operations through a single, master routine or service.
Avoid logging sensitive information that could compromise system security.
Establish a secure, centralized log analysis mechanism to monitor and respond to security events.
All input validation failures must be logged with sufficient detail to support security monitoring and incident response.
Log all authentication attempts, including both successes and failures, to ensure proper monitoring and incident response.
Log all access control failures to provide a traceable audit trail of authorization decisions.
Log all apparent tampering events, including unexpected changes to state data, for effective detection and forensic analysis.
Log attempts to use invalid or expired session tokens, ensuring sensitive token values are not recorded.
All system exceptions must be logged securely with sufficient detail to support debugging and incident response while protecting sensitive data.
Log all administrative actions, including changes to security configurations, to ensure auditability and accountability.
All backend TLS connection failures must be logged in detail to support operational monitoring and security incident detection.
Ensure all failures occurring within cryptographic modules are securely and comprehensively logged.
Implement cryptographic hash functions, ideally with an HMAC, to ensure the integrity and non-repudiation of log entries.
Enforce the principle of least privilege to limit user access rights.
Ensure sensitive data in temporary storage is protected and purged promptly.
Encrypt highly sensitive stored information at rest using vetted cryptographic algorithms to prevent unauthorized access.
Prevent exposure of server-side source code to clients by ensuring proper server configuration and access controls.
Sensitive information should never be stored in clear text or insecure formats on the client side.
Remove comments in production code that may expose sensitive backend details.
Minimize or restrict access to unnecessary application and system documentation to mitigate information disclosure risks.
Sensitive information must never be transmitted via HTTP GET request parameters.
Disable autocomplete on forms handling sensitive information, including authentication credentials.
Always disable client-side caching for pages that handle sensitive data.
Ensure the secure deletion of sensitive data when it is no longer needed across all storage layers.
Enforce strict access controls on all sensitive data stored on the server, including cached and temporary data, ensuring only authorized system users or processes can access it.
Encrypt all sensitive data during transmission using TLS and additional encryption as necessary.
Ensure all TLS certificates are valid, unexpired, correctly match the domain, and include necessary intermediate certificates for proper chain validation.
Do not downgrade a failed TLS connection to an insecure channel; if TLS negotiation fails, abort the connection rather than falling back to plaintext.
Use TLS for secure communication of sensitive data.
All connections to external systems that transmit or process sensitive information or invoke privileged functions must use TLS to ensure confidentiality and integrity.
Use a single well-configured TLS implementation for all secure communications.
Always define character encodings for data transmission to ensure consistent interpretation of data.
Always strip sensitive parameters from URLs to prevent exposure in HTTP Referer headers when linking to external sites.
Always keep servers, frameworks, and system components updated to the latest approved and patched versions to mitigate known vulnerabilities.
Maintain all servers, frameworks, and system components by applying the latest security patches and updates available.
Disable directory listings to prevent exposing sensitive server files and structures.
Enforce least privilege for web server, processes, and service accounts.
Always handle exceptions in a way that prevents sensitive information exposure and maintains system security.
Minimize the attack surface by removing all unnecessary functionality, services, and files from production systems.
Remove all test code, debug backdoors, and non-production functionality before deploying to a production environment to minimize attack surfaces.
Do not disclose internal directory structure in robots.txt; place non-public directories under a single parent and disallow that parent rather than enumerating each directory.
Explicitly define and enforce the exact HTTP methods supported for each endpoint.
Disable all unnecessary HTTP methods (e.g., WebDAV extensions like PUT, DELETE, PROPFIND) and require strong authentication for any extended file-handling methods that must remain enabled.
Ensure consistent configuration of HTTP protocol versions on the web server.
Eliminate sensitive information from HTTP response headers to prevent information leakage.
Security configurations must be easily auditable in a human-readable format.
Establish and maintain an asset management system that comprehensively tracks all system components and software configurations.
Isolate development environments from production networks and restrict access to authorized development and testing personnel.
All code changes in development and production must be managed and recorded through a formal software change control system.
Always use strongly typed parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection vulnerabilities when handling user inputs.
Always validate and encode all input—including meta characters—before executing any database command, and abort execution if validation or encoding fails.
All variables interacting with data stores must be explicitly and strongly typed to avoid type confusion and vulnerabilities.
Always use the minimal privileges necessary for database access.
Use strong, secure, and centrally managed credentials for database connections and protect them from exposure.
Connection strings must never be hardcoded within application source code and should instead be securely stored in an encrypted configuration file.
Use stored procedures to encapsulate data access and enable least-privilege by revoking direct permissions on base tables.
Database connections must be closed immediately after use to release resources and minimize exposure to attacks.
Always replace default database administrative passwords with strong, unique credentials or implement multi-factor authentication.
Minimize database functionality to reduce attack vectors.
All unnecessary default vendor content, including sample schemas and demo accounts, must be removed before deploying a database to any environment.
Disable or remove all default accounts from the database that are not specifically needed for legitimate operations.
Use distinct database credentials for different user roles to enforce least privilege.
Avoid directly using user-supplied input in dynamic file inclusions to prevent unauthorized access and code execution.
Require user authentication prior to any file upload operations to ensure only authorized users can submit files.
Limit uploads to only the allowed file types required for legitimate business purposes through robust server-side validation.
Always validate uploaded files by checking their headers to ensure they are of the expected type, not just relying on file extensions.
Files must be stored outside the application's web context, utilizing dedicated content servers or database storage to prevent direct access.
Restrict file uploads to validated types to mitigate risks of server execution of malicious files.
Disable execution privileges in file upload directories to prevent execution of uploaded files.
Ensure secure file uploads by utilizing chrooted environments or logical drive mounting to restrict unauthorized access.
Always validate file names and types against a whitelist to prevent unauthorized file access.
Avoid passing user-supplied data into dynamic redirects without strict validation.
Avoid passing arbitrary file paths; instead, use predefined index values.
Applications must never expose absolute file paths to clients.
Application files and resources must be set to read-only permissions to prevent unauthorized modifications and maintain integrity.
All files uploaded by users must be scanned for viruses and malware before being processed, stored, or made available to other users.
Always validate and sanitize untrusted input and output to prevent vulnerabilities.
Always ensure that allocated buffers are sufficiently sized to prevent overflows.
Always ensure that bounded string copy functions like strncpy() result in a NULL-terminated destination buffer.
Always validate buffer boundaries, particularly within iterative operations, to prevent memory corruption and buffer overflows.
Always truncate input strings to a safe, bounded length before passing them to string copy or concatenation functions to prevent buffer overflows.
Always explicitly close resources such as file handles and connection objects rather than relying on garbage collection to release them.
Enable non-executable stack protections (NX/DEP) to prevent execution of injected code.
Avoid using known vulnerable functions that can lead to memory corruption and security vulnerabilities by replacing them with safer alternatives.
Always release allocated memory to prevent memory leaks at every function exit path.
Prefer well-tested, approved managed libraries and frameworks for common tasks instead of writing custom unmanaged code that bypasses runtime safety guarantees.
Use task-specific built-in APIs for OS operations instead of issuing direct shell commands.
Always verify the integrity of code and files using checksums or cryptographic hashes before execution.
Always use locks or synchronization mechanisms to protect shared resources from concurrent access that could cause race conditions.
Ensure shared variables and resources are protected against inappropriate concurrent access.
Always explicitly initialize all variables and data stores at declaration or before first use to prevent unpredictable behavior and information leakage.
Minimize the duration of elevated privileges in your application.

Prevent numeric calculation errors by thoroughly understanding and accounting for your language's numeric representation limits, type conversions, overflow, underflow, precision loss, and signed/unsigned distinctions.
Never pass user-supplied data directly to dynamic execution functions.
Prevent unauthorized users from generating or modifying application code.
Thoroughly review and validate all third-party components and libraries for business necessity and security before integration.
Ensure secure automatic updates through verification and encryption.
